problem: Embodied navigation agents are rarely tested for adversarial robustness. Per-timestep RL observation attacks (FGSM-style, SA-MDP, two-stage attacks) must compute a new perturbation at every step, which is impractical when the attacker cannot hack the running system. Standard universal adversarial perturbations (UAP) assume i.i.d. images, so they ignore the MDP dynamics that link frames in one trajectory.
motivation: A single image-agnostic perturbation added to every frame is cheap and realistic to deploy (e.g., a patch stuck on the sensor). For embodied agents that must act safely in the real world, that makes it the most worrying threat. The Disturbed Policy Gradient theorem shows that a navigation UAP should weight each state-action gradient by its disturbed Q value. Naive UAP simply averages per-frame gradients, which suggests it is sub-optimal.
key_idea: Model a constant observation perturbation as a δ-disturbed MDP and optimize δ to minimize the agent's disturbed return. The gradient comes from a policy-gradient-style estimator weighted by Q (Reward UAP) or by a goal-success signal (Trajectory UAP), using trajectories collected under the current perturbation.
insight: The disturbed policy gradient ∇δJδ = 1/(1−γ)·E_{s∼dδ,a∼π(·|s+δ)}[Qδ(s,a)∇ log π(a|s+δ)] has two consequences. Samples must come from the disturbed state distribution, hence iterative re-sampling under the current δ. Gradients must also be weighted by long-horizon value rather than averaged uniformly. With few trajectories (5), the sparse goal-only signal of Trajectory UAP gives a lower-variance Q estimate and is usually strongest on Gibson and MP3D. The m-ablation (Table 2, Habitat-test, depth) shows Reward UAP improving sharply with more samples: at m=15 it drops victim Succ to 0.16 vs 0.49 for standard UAP, where at m=5 all three attacks were about equal (~0.48-0.49). So the gains come from a better gradient estimate as sample size grows. Standard UAP does not benefit from more samples.
method: δ-MDP formulation: the same noise δ is added to every observation, so the victim acts with π(·|s+δ) while dynamics and reward use the true state; this equals the disturbed policy πδ interacting with the original MDP; objective δ* = argmin_{δ∈B_p(0,ε)} Jδ(π).

Disturbed Bellman equation and Disturbed Policy Gradient theorem: ∇δJδ(π) expressed via Qδ(s,a)·∇_{s+δ} log π(a|s+δ) over the disturbed discounted state distribution, computable by backprop through the victim network (white-box).

Multi-step optimization: at each iteration k, collect l trajectories with the current disturbed policy πδk, take a gradient-descent step on δ, repeat for n iterations (m = n·l trajectories), then project δ to the boundary of the ε l2-ball (δ = ε δ/||δ||).
Reward UAP: estimates Qδ with the discounted reward-to-go of sampled trajectories, or with the victim's own Q function, and updates δ ← δ − α Σ_i Σ_t R̂_t ∇ log πδ(a_t|s_t).

Trajectory UAP: treats navigation as a goal-conditioned MDP with a binary success reward, so Qg(s_t,a_t) = γ^{T−t}·g (g = 1 if the goal is reached). Only success/failure is needed, not the dense distance-based reward, and the estimate is lower variance.
Baseline 'UAP in MDP': minimizes the probability of the victim's original argmax action over states from undisturbed victim rollouts, treating frames as i.i.d.

setting.backbone: Victims: official pre-trained habitat-baselines PPO PointGoal agents (RGB or Depth), frozen; the attack is a gradient-optimized perturbation using white-box gradients of the victim policy
setting.training_data: No victim training. The perturbation is optimized from only 5 trajectories sampled with the (disturbed) victim policy in the main table, and 5/10/15 trajectories in the ablation. Victims are the officially released habitat-baselines checkpoints.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB or depth (separate victims) + PointGoal target (GPS/compass-style goal vector as in habitat-baselines)
setting.action_space: discrete Habitat PointNav actions of the victim (forward/turn/stop); max 500 actions per episode
setting.privileged: Attacker has white-box gradient access to the victim policy and uses the reward signal (Reward UAP) or the success signal (Trajectory UAP) from rollouts. The victim itself uses no privileged information.

numbers_note: This is an adversarial-attack paper. All numbers are the frozen victim agent's performance under the attack, so lower means a stronger attack. The paper prints Succ and SPL as fractions (e.g., 0.16); they are converted here to 0-100. 'Rew' is average episode reward. The paper does not name the dataset splits: Gibson (994 episodes) and MP3D (495 episodes) match the standard PointNav val sets, and Habitat-test uses 100 episodes. Table 2 ablates the number of trajectories m on Habitat-test with the depth victim: m=10 gives Reward UAP -1.57/0.43/0.28 and Trajectory UAP -1.22/0.45/0.32; m=15 gives Reward UAP -4.15/0.16/0.12, Trajectory UAP -1.11/0.47/0.32, and standard UAP -0.60/0.49/0.36. No seeds or variance are reported.
results: All attacks sharply degrade the pre-trained habitat-baselines PPO PointGoal agents. Trajectory UAP drives success near zero in most settings: Gibson-Depth Succ 0.92→0.05 vs 0.44 for standard UAP, and MP3D-Depth 0.80→0.01 vs 0.04. On RGB, Trajectory UAP reaches Habitat-test Succ 0.05 vs 0.13 for UAP. Gains over the standard-UAP baseline are not uniform: on MP3D-RGB, UAP already reaches 0.00 Succ, and on Habitat-test-Depth all methods sit at ~0.48-0.49 with 5 trajectories. With 15 trajectories, Reward UAP clearly wins there (0.16 vs 0.49).
limitations: White-box setting: requires gradients of the victim policy plus reward or success signals from rollouts. The perturbation is purely digital, and physical realizability (e.g., the sensor patch) is not tested.
Only PointGoal navigation with the older habitat-baselines PPO victims (RGB or Depth separately). No stronger agents (e.g., DD-PPO), other tasks, or defenses are evaluated.
Advantage over the naive UAP baseline is inconsistent: it ties or loses in some settings (MP3D-RGB, Habitat-test-Depth at m=5). Results are single runs, and Habitat-test has only 100 episodes.
builds_on: Adversarial attacks on neural network policies (Huang et al. 2017)
compares_to: Standard UAP extended to MDP (frames treated as i.i.d.)
